newsitem.title: INDIA: India massacres cap decades of ethnic turmoil.
newsitem.headline: India massacres cap decades of ethnic turmoil.

text.p: A surge in ethnic violence in northeast India caps decades of festering hostility between the region's tribesmen and settlers from neighbouring Bangladesh, analysts said on Monday.
They said the attacks appeared aimed at changing the demographic balance in the fertile, hilly state which shares a porous, poorly-policed frontier with Bangladesh on three sides.

At least 35 people died in an eruption of arson and murder early on Sunday, and army and paramilitary soldiers enforcing an indefinite curfew in Tripura's tense Khowai region bordering Bangladesh have been given orders to shoot rioters on sight.

"This is a clear case of attempted ethnic cleansing. The tribespeople who were once the majority in Tripura are now outnumbered almost three to one and this is a situation many of them cannot accept," said a former police official with long experience in the region who did not wish to be identified.
Tripura was a princely state until it joined the Indian union in 1949, two years after the nation won freedom from Britain and the subcontinent was divided between India and Pakistan.

Bengali Hindus began to pour into Tripura from the former East Pakistan, now Bangladesh. By the 1970s, the Bengalis had become a decisive majority in the population of about three million and controlled much of the farming land, jobs and businesses.

"That's why we went into the jungles to fight. No one likes his land to be taken over by foreign settlers," said Bijoy Kumar Hrangkhawl, who led a decade-long bush war at the head of a ragtag guerrilla army called the Tripura National Volunteers.
Hrangkhawl decided to come out of the jungles when the Indian government set up a Tripura tribal areas autonomous district council in 1985, promising autonomy to the tribesmen.
"But it has fallen short of our expectations. We have got nothing," said Sabda Kumar Jamatia, a tribal student leader.

The killings have provoked retaliation from the Bengalis. On Sunday they attacked a tribal village and killed three people. "We cannot take these mass murders lying down. We will hit back," said Haripada Sarkar, who leads the Amra Bangalee (We are Bengalis), a militant group of settlers.
Since 1980, when over 2,000 people died in rioting between Bengali settlers and tribal militants, Tripura has been gripped by periodic outbursts of ethnic mayhem.

The violence subsided after Hrangkhawl and his guerrillas surrendered in 1988, but four years later two new rebel groups -- the National Liberation Front of Tripura and the All Tripura Tiger Force (ATTF) -- launched a fresh round of attacks on Bengalis.

In June 1996 the ATTF asked Bengalis to quit the state. Over 90 people have died in sporadic attacks on Bengali settlements since December, and Sunday's violence, in which tribal attackers torched homes in three villages and shot residents when they fled, marked the worst outbreak.
Ethnic hatred is convulsing other parts of India's remote northeast, which abuts Bangladesh and Burma.
"It's a game of numbers and territory, a fight over scarce resources, land and language and leadership," the former police official said.
"A small community loses land to settlers, their language and culture are overshadowed, they lose out in the race for leadership and all these add to collective anger," he said.
Land and development form Tripura's friction points. Nearly a half-century after its tribal ruler acceded to India, the state has only a small railway and no major industries.

"The Bengalis, who came in after (the 1947) partition, eyed the fertile land in Tripura because there was little else to invest in. The tribespeople lost out in competition and are now trying to recover what they lost," said economist Jalad Ganguly.

Tripura's Marxist government has tried to reduce the potential for conflict. The state was given a $2.0 million loan by the World Bank to develop rubber plantations and wean the tribespeople away from unproductive slash-and-burn cultivation techniques.
"But rubber is a difficult crop, needs a lot of attention and advice and our experts are scared of going into the hills now," said A.K. Krishna Kumar of the Rubber Production Commission.
